text.en: Meena sees mist above a cup of tea and ice in a glass of juice. She wonders how to compare the drinks without touching them. A thermometer can give a temperature reading.

Our sense of touch cannot give an exact temperature. Two hands can feel the same water differently if one hand was cooler beforehand. To measure how hot or cold something is, we use temperature.
Temperature tells us how hot or cold an object is. Heat is energy transferred because of a difference in temperature. Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.
A clinical thermometer is designed to measure body temperature. Many modern clinical thermometers are digital, with a number shown on a display. Laboratory thermometers have different ranges. One example has a scale from minus 10 to 110 degrees Celsius. Normal human body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius.
Glass thermometers containing mercury are an older design. Do not handle one. Use an instrument your teacher provides for a science demonstration, such as a suitable mercury-free thermometer. In a supervised demonstration with a mercury-free liquid thermometer, the bulb stays in the water away from the sides and bottom. The scale is read at eye level. Never hold a clinical thermometer in hot water.

If two people disagree about whether a room feels warm, a temperature reading gives them something they can both check. The reading describes the air, even if their hands feel different.
Suppose a cool object sits beside a warmer one and touches it. Energy can move from the warmer object to the cooler one. Temperature helps us describe the difference that drives the transfer.

board.text: Energy moves from warmer to cooler

text.en: Look at a thermometer diagram with marked lines at twenty, twenty-two, twenty-four and twenty-six degrees Celsius. Notice how many degrees there are between neighbouring marks.
Each marked step is two degrees. If the column reaches halfway between twenty-two and twenty-four, its reading is about twenty-three degrees Celsius.
Some scales show temperatures below zero. On a diagram labelled minus two, zero and two, minus two is lower than zero, and two is higher.
On a liquid thermometer diagram, read where the top of the column sits beside the scale. In a demonstration, your teacher looks at that height so the line seems to match the correct mark.

board.text: Read the top of the liquid column

text.en: Looking from above or below can make the mark appear to shift. That reading error is called parallax. Eye level helps us avoid it.
Look at the smallest and largest numbers printed on the thermometer. Those limits describe its range. A classroom example might be marked from minus ten to one hundred ten degrees Celsius.
If an instrument’s scale stops at fifty degrees, it cannot give a reading of seventy on that scale. Choose an instrument designed for the measurement and its expected range.

board.text: Choose a range that covers the measurement

text.en: A digital thermometer uses a display. Some digital instruments are made for body temperature, and others are designed for experiments or weather. They are selected for different jobs.

board.text: Match the instrument to the job

text.en: A red liquid column in a classroom drawing shows another kind of display. An old mercury thermometer can be hazardous if it breaks. Leave it alone and let an adult deal with it.
Imagine your teacher comparing a cup of room-temperature water with a cup of cooler water, using the same suitable mercury-free instrument. Predict which reading will be lower.

board.text: Compare two cups with the same instrument

text.en: Your teacher keeps the sensing part in the water and away from the cup walls and bottom. Touching the cup can affect the reading if the cup is at a different temperature.

board.text: Sense the water away from the cup wall

text.en: A thermometer reading may change at first as the sensor adjusts. Your teacher waits for it to settle, then reads it according to the instrument’s directions.

board.text: Wait for the reading to settle

text.en: Our example readings are twenty-two degrees for the first cup and sixteen degrees for the cooler cup. Record the cup name, the reading and the unit so someone else can compare.
Cup B is cooler because sixteen is lower than twenty-two. The difference is six degrees Celsius. A difference compares two readings.
If you want the temperature of outdoor air, a thermometer left in direct sunshine can warm up. A thermometer used for weather is normally shielded from direct sunlight while air can flow past it.
To compare outdoor readings at different times, keep the instrument in the same suitable place and write down the time of each reading.

board.text: Record the place and time with each reading

text.en: A reading of twenty-five degrees at midday and twenty degrees later shows the air at that spot was cooler at the later time. It does not tell us what happened at every place nearby.
When you hear a temperature reading, ask what was measured, which scale was used and when or where the reading was taken. Those details give the number its meaning.

problem.en: One sample reads 37 degrees Celsius and another reads 39. What is the difference between their temperatures?

text.en: Subtract 37 from 39.
The difference is 2 degrees Celsius.

why.en: Both readings use the same scale.

prompt.en: Why can you not trust your hand to measure temperature?

requiredIdeas.en: The hand feels relative to its own state.
A thermometer gives a number everyone can agree on.

points.en: Touch is unreliable; use a thermometer.
Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.
A clinical thermometer measures body temperature.
Read a liquid-in-glass thermometer at eye level during supervised measurement.
